Description: Satellite measurements of volcanic sulfur dioxide (so2) and ash emissions are crucial for detection of volcanic eruptions and for quantifying volcanic impacts on the atmosphere and climate. volcanic so2 and ash emissions have been measured BY Ultraviolet (UV) and infrared (IR) sensors on polar-orbiting satellites since the late 1970s, but with poor temporal resolution. several geostationary IR sensors CAN detect volcanic ash and so2, but with lower sensitivity than UV measurements, especially in the lower troposphere. this has limited our ability to study key processes during the initial few hours of atmospheric residence of volcanic eruption clouds. in 2015, the launch of the Earth Polychromatic Imaging Camera (EPIC) aboard the Deep Space Climate Observatory (DSCOVR) provided the FIRST opportunity to observe volcanic eruption clouds globally from the L1 earth-sun lagrange point. EPIC is a 10-channel UV   NEAR IR spectroradiometer that provides sunrise-sunset earth observations with a cadence of 68-110 minutes depending on season, with calibrated EPIC UV radiances available for level 2 (l2) retrievals of trace gases including ozone and so2 and calculation of a UV aerosol index (AI) that is sensitive to volcanic ash. EPIC hence offers the potential for multiple daily observations of volcanic so2 and ash clouds in its field of view. EPIC s unique ability to provide high-cadence UV observations of volcanic eruption clouds has been demonstrated in several recent volcanic eruptions. the increased observation frequency of DSCOVR/EPIC will permit more timely volcanic eruption detection, improved trajectory modeling, and novel analyses of the temporal evolution of volcanic clouds. an opportunity to explore the potential of a new earth observation paradigm and its application to remote sensing of volcanic clouds is rare. from L1, EPIC s observation frequency is intermediate between polar-orbiting (LEO) and geostationary (GEO) sensors, but is the highest temporal resolution of UV satellite measurements achieved to date. EPIC covers the entire sunlit earth disk and more of the polar regions than GEO sensors in the summer months, and partly fills a ~4-hour daytime measurement gap between overpasses of sun-synchronous LEO weather satellites at ~9:30 am (e.g., the european metop-a/b satellites) and ~1:30 PM local time (e.g., NASA s aqua, aura and suomi-npp satellites), and also collects data later into the afternoon. under prior DSCOVR science team support our group has developed an EPIC so2 retrieval algorithm that has successfully detected at least 12 significant volcanic eruptions since 2015. our so2 team at michigan tech and NASA GSFC has unique, multi-decadal experience in measuring so2 from volcanic eruptions from space using UV satellite instruments (http://so2.GSFC.NASA.gov). in this project we propose to continue development and maintenance of the EPIC so2 algorithm and derived l2 products, and conduct detailed validation and scientific analysis of EPIC so2 and AI retrievals following several of these and future volcanic eruptions to demonstrate how these unique observations CAN advance our understanding of volcanic cloud processes (e.g., the lifetimes of, and interactions between, so2 and ash on hourly timescales) and impacts. we propose the following specific activities under this proposal: - continued maintenance of the DSCOVR/EPIC so2 algorithm and production of level 2 EPIC volcanic so2 and AI data products for the user community - evaluation and validation of EPIC so2 and aerosol index (AI) data for volcanic eruptions with other LEO UV and IR satellite so2 measurements (e.g., omi, OMPS, AIRS) - scientific analysis of EPIC so2 and AI data for a selection of well-characterized volcanic eruptions (both explosive and effusive) using trajectory and chemical-transport modeling - promotion and public dissemination of the unique capabilities of EPIC observations via websites and social media.

Description: Midlatitude extreme weather events such AS cold air outbreaks, heat WAVES, floods and droughts are responsible for disproportionately large climate-related damage. in recent decades extremes were caused BY anthropogenic climate change or internal variability in the climate system. we propose to develop a comprehensive understanding of atmospheric processes responsible for changes forcings, and the role of the stratosphere in the unforced and forced variability. we plan to FIRST extend our previous work on local rossby wave activity to a unified set of dynamics-based metrics Measurement (GPM). then, we will use these metrics to evaluate midlatitude subseasonal and interannual atmospheric variability in several ensembles of climate model simulations. in particular, we will analyze GISS model e2.1/e2.2 simulations on the influence of the stratosphere on surface extreme events. finally, we will examine the coupled model intercomparison project phase 6 (cmip6) simulations of midlatitude extremes in the historical period, in the NEAR future, and at the end of the 21st century. the proposed research directly addresses the theme of extremes in the earth system  in the transport, and their impacts on temperature and precipitation extremes are properly represented in earth system models we strive to understand the role of internal variability, BY collaborating with GISS and JPL scientists, this will contribute to NASA s modeling efforts through the use of satellite retrievals of water vapor and precipitation AS observational constraints of midlatitude circulation and moisture transport in climate models.

Description: The suomi-npp and JPSS albedo, brdf and nbar products have been developed to provide long-term climate-quality continuity with the more than two decades of modis products provided BY the terra and aqua missions. land surface albedo is an essential climate variable (ecv), required BY climate, weather, hydrologic, and biogeochemical modelers to quantify the reflective character of land surfaces, and thus estimate the surface radiative forcing. land surface albedo varies widely in space and time, and is dependent on the land cover, vegetation structure, seasonal phenology, vegetation condition and health, snow cover, and disturbance. the VIIRS products, from the suomi-npp and the JPSS (currently NOAA-20) missions, provide daily gridded global estimates of this surface variability AS both standard products and AS LANCE nrt products. in comparisons with tower albedo data from spatially representative sites, they have been shown to capture the rapid daily variations in albedo caused BY ephemeral snowfall and melt, seasonal phenological changes, and disturbance. the intrinsic surface reflectance anisotropy is determined BY fitting bidirectional reflectance distribution function (brdf) models to multi-angle cloud-free satellite reflectance observations of each grid location. these brdf estimates, are then integrated hemispherically over all view and illumination geometries to generate intrinsic white sky albedo (bihemispherical reflectance) and over all view angles at a particular SOLAR zenith angle to generate black sky albedo (directional-hemispherical reflectance at local SOLAR noon). the brdf quantities are also used to correct directional surface reflectances to a common view angle (e.g. the nadir brdf-adjusted surface reflectances (nbar) product) and to estimate measures of surface canopy clumping and structure. the standard VIIRS view-angle-corrected nbar product (provided at local SOLAR noon) are also used to generate downstream uncertainty information and these high-quality products are being embraced BY global and regional modeling and monitoring communities to extend the long term record, begun with the modis instruments, into the future. thus, this effort is focused on the continued maintenance of heritage suomi-npp and JPSS VIIRS albedo, brdf and nbar products to provide a consistent climate quality record of the radiative character of the earth s land surfaces.

Description: Earth s energy imbalance, currently estimated at 0.8 0.2 w m-2, is stored primarily in the ocean and is a key contributor to sea level rise. while global mean sea level has risen at a rate of 3.4 mm/year since 1993, regional deviations have been substantial, leading to marginal rates of rise in some locations while doubling rates in others. an understanding of these spatial patterns and the relative roles of internal variability and forced changes in driving them is critical for providing actionable guidance on changes over the coming decade and beyond. given sea level s strong ties to the energy budget, a multidisciplinary effort is proposed, combining data based on terra and aqua satellite observations, along with complementary NASA reanalysis data (merra-2, eccov4), and satellite altimetry with the overarching goal of quantifying the drivers of regional sea level rise in nature and improving the representation and prediction of these drivers in climate models. the specific goals of this proposal are to 1) use terra and aqua data to quantify the flows of energy that DRIVE regional sea level rise during the altimeter era AS PART of a novel and holistic observational analysis that combines satellite retrievals with atmospheric and ocean reanalyses, and 2) use this analysis to assess ncar and NASA climate model simulations, identify their dominant biases, and inform model development and projections. the proposal is motivated in PART BY recent studies BY the pis revealing the emergence of the climate-change forced response in regional sea level in altimetry data and the associated predictable component of rise in the coming decades. based on these results, it is argued that the flows of energy through the climate system diagnosed from terra, aqua, and complementary data, and forced changes estimated from models, in addition to being a powerful constraint on model feedbacks, CAN serve AS the basis for multidecadal regional sea level rise predictions. the FIRST stage of our proposed work lies in diagnosing terra/aqua-era regional sea level rise, including its steric and DYNAMIC contributions and the associated atmospheric, surface, and oceanic energy fluxes that DRIVE them. we will use top-of-atmosphere and surface radiative fluxes provided BY the clouds and earth RADIANT energy system (CERES) project. we will also use a new CERES product, the radiative flux BY cloud type (fct) dataset, based on CERES and modis measurements on terra and aqua, to provide a detailed understanding of the role of clouds in these budgets. the merra-2 reanalyses will also be used to provide estimates of flows within the atmosphere. ocean budgets will be closed with ocean state estimation from both the estimating the circulation and climate of the ocean (ecco) project. ancillary data products (e.g. deepc), which have been generated using other satellites anchored BY CERES, will also be used to extend our analysis back in time to 1993, the beginning of the altimeter era. a priority will be given to understanding the influence of advances in the observing system such AS argo to the time-varying uncertainty in these data. in turn, these diagnostics will be used to assess ncar and NASA climate models, including their simulated modes of internal variability and forced responses to climate change. models from other u.s. modeling centers may also be assessed, AS the necessary data become available. a central focus of our model evaluation exercise will be on the radiative flux contributions of various cloud types using the fct simulator. in an effort to better understand the drivers of variability in the altimeter record, single-forcing simulations from ncar s cesm1 and cesm2, and NASA s GISS-model-e will be used, both during the altimeter era and further back in time. lastly, and based on the ability of climate models to the altimeter record of regional SLR and its drivers, Machine Learning methods will be used to winnow projections from climate models.

Description: Recent recognition that land-atmosphere interactions constitute one of the greatest sources of climate uncertainty at 7-30 day timescales has pushed land-atmosphere interactions research to the forefront of earth system model development. climate modelprojected warming and drying trends in many midlatitude land regions underscore the pressing need to better understand the potential contributing role of land atmosphere interactions to these trends. for example, it is critical to understand the sensitivity of land  atmosphere coupling to potential future changes in: landcover and growing season length, temperature and humidity, precipitation and evaporation, and atmospheric circulations. however, limited long-term observational data records of land atmosphere coupling across diverse climate zones limits the extent to which climate model coupled process parameterization may be constrained. we propose to demonstrate that the long-term, integrated multi-satellite, multi-sensor satellite records of NASA s terra, aqua, suomi npp, and NOAA-20 CAN address this data gap through their use in quantification and process attribution of historical land atmosphere coupling variability and trends. the proposed project will address the following specific questions: 1. what is the regional frequency and subseasonal to interannual variability of locally-forced weather events across midlatitudes? 2. to what extent is the frequency of locally-forced weather explained BY vegetation and seasonality? 3. to what extent is land atmosphere coupling strength explained BY weather regime sequencing? 4. how has locally-forced weather contributed to hydroclimate and the evolution of past droughts? 5. how well DO conclusions based on temporally coarse but spatially extensive satellite-based data compare with conclusions supported only BY regional in situ surface-based point observations? the project design is two-pronged with a regional in situ data track and a global satellite data track. the satellite track begins with production of a FIRST-of-its-kind Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS)-era (2002-2019) 1x1 degree daily reanalysis of midlatitude land-atmosphere coupling, which is subsequently used in a series of increasingly finer time resolution studies, from all-season (year 1) to seasonal (year 2), to 3 7 day synoptic event (year 3) bases. BY contrast, the in situ studies cover all three analysis time scales for a given land-atmosphere coupling hot spot during each project year. in these hotspots, modeling studies have indicated an outsized impact of soil moisture realism on subseasonal temperature and precipitation prediction. the diverse ecosystems and hydroclimates of the hot spots affects land atmosphere coupling variability, and potentially, its detectability from the coarse satellite sensors. BY design, the hot spots are studied in order of decreasing data availability: u.s. GREAT plains, eastern u.s. forests, and south american pampas. accordingly, the in situ data track serves AS a key source of project risk mitigation to the extent that it helps to define minimum satellite data requirements (i.e., observations and temporal sampling) for detecting land-atmosphere coupling variability in different regions. pending the success of our AIRS-era analyses, we will pursue an extension of the satellite track studies back to 1983 using hirs (high-resolution infrared radiation sounder) and other complimentary sensor records. the novel interdisciplinary approaches and datasets of this work will pave the way for accelerated application of NASA satellite data in studies of land atmosphere interaction, refinement of coupled land atmospheric process representation in models, and ultimately, improved weather and climate prediction.

Description: Global chemistry climate models (ccms) show a large spread in their simulated distributions of key tropospheric constituents, including the hydroxyl radical (oh), the atmosphere s primary oxidant. ccms are one of the primary tools for investigating chemistry climate feedbacks such AS the 2-way interaction of methane lifetime, which is largely controlled BY oh, with climate. understanding the causes of inter-model spread in oh is therefore vital to reducing uncertainties in chemistry-climate feedbacks on methane lifetime AS well AS in the simulation of the many atmospheric constituents that are influenced BY oh. while oh itself is too short-lived to undergo significant transport, its distribution is strongly related to that of its chemical drivers, such AS ozone, water vapor, carbon monoxide (co), and nitrogen dioxide (no2), which undergo transport and for which space-based observational constraints are available. we propose a comprehensive approach to identify how differences in key model dynamical processes manifest in differences in the simulated distributions of the chemical drivers of oh and, subsequently, oh itself. we will investigate how inter-model differences in dynamics impact simulated oh. while recent work has focused primarily on the impact of differences in chemical processes, we focus on dynamics because of its important role in setting the distribution of the chemical drivers of oh. we propose to re-cast the oh sensitivities in terms of the DYNAMIC and meteorological drivers of oh sources and sinks. we will employ statistical analyses, including a Machine Learning technique, to identify relationships between meteorology, idealized TRACERS, and simulated oh across the models in a recent model intercomparison. we will also use sensitivity studies with a single model to quantify the role of specific processes identified in the statistical analysis. a key deliverable of the proposed work will be a description of novel, process-based diagnostics, based on satellite observations and idealized TRACERS, that may be used to identify the potential contribution of a dynamical process to inter-model differences in the distributions of oh and its chemical drivers. we will take advantage of long-term satellite data records, including recent multi-satellite datasets, to develop diagnostics for assessing the credibility of the simulated chemical drivers of oh. we propose to use observations from NASA satellites including EOS aura (tes, mls, omi), aqua (AIRS), and terra (mopitt) for this work. our proposed work aims to address the following questions:   how DO differences in simulated transport impact the simulated spatial distributions of the chemical drivers of oh and, subsequently, oh?   how DO differences in the simulation of interannual variability related to enso and other climate indices manifest in the variability of the drivers of oh and oh itself?   what does comparison of simulated outgoing longwave radiation (olr), cloud cover, no2, co, ozone, and water vapor with satellite observations indicate about the credibility of simulated oh variability? it directly addresses the aura/acmap research issues of tropospheric air quality and oxidation efficiency and chemistry/climate interactions.

Description: The goal of this project is to advance the development of the hitran (high-resolution transmission) molecular spectroscopic database compilation and associated software. the database is critical for the NASA observation missions that seek to characterize the atmosphere using remote sensing experiments, primarily from space. these missions consist of the suite of former and current NASA experiments, including instruments on aura (hirdls, mls, tes, and omi) AS well AS AIRS, mopitt, SAGE III, oco-2 and oco-3, aqua, terra, EMIT, ECOSTRESS and future approved or proposed NASA missions including TEMPO, libera, CLARREO, GEO-cape, gacm, PACE. this project also benefits from a close relationship with non-NASA and foreign missions, including ACE, tropomi, gosat (1 and 2), iasi, toms, sbuv, jem/smiles, gems, gome on ers-2, sciamachy and gomos flying on envisat, smr on odin, cris instrument flying on suomi npp, NOAA-20 and noaa21 AS well AS future non-NASA missions, including merlin, iasi-NG, carbonsat, methanesat and microcarb. NASA airborne science program, AS well AS, the ground-based tccon and ndacc networks, also rely on the quality of the reference spectroscopic data. it is FAIR to say that every NASA-funded mission equipped with spectrometers of any resolution use hitran data in the analyses of their retrievals. the priority of the program is to improve the spectroscopic parameters of molecular transitions that affect the Modeling and Simulation of atmospheric radiance and transmission retrievals. particular goals include improved accuracy of all spectroscopic parameters, global consistency of line intensities, improved line-shape parameters (and the means BY which they are represented), the addition of missing molecular bands and trace gas species, representation of phenomena that are impacting the retrievals, including collision-induced absorption (CIA) bands, advanced line-shape formalisms, line mixing, and water vapor continuum. realistic uncertainty estimates, along with the links to the original data sources, will also be provided. the tools for disseminating and working with the data, including the online interface and hitran Application Programming Interface (hapi) will also be improved and enhanced. user support, advanced documentation, and tutorials, AS well AS an improved interface for NASA projects, are thus INTEGRAL aspects of the hitran project. in summary, the database will develop following the pact (practical, accurate, complete, and traceable) approach.

Description: A proposal for maintaining the current s-npp and NOAA-20 fusion radiance products to provide continuity with aqua modis measurements. AS background for the VIIRS+cris fusion radiance product, modis has three bands sensitive to co2 around 4.3  m and another four around 15  m, two bands sensitive to h2o NEAR 6.7  m, and a band sensitive to ozone NEAR 9.6  m.
